newsitem.title: UK: Sterling debt and futures closing report.
newsitem.headline: Sterling debt and futures closing report.

text.p: Gilts ended almost unchanged on Tuesday but nearly a half-point off their lows with key retail sales data and the first gilt auction of the new financial year, both due on Wednesday, casting a pall over the markets.
The June gilt future settled at 109-13, down 1/32 on the day having meandered between 109-07 and 109-16 for the whole session.
"We've had a pretty lethargic day and you're looking at a 109-06 to 109-18, 20 range until the sales figures and the auction have been and gone," said Jonathan York, broker at MeesPierson.

Retail sales are forecast to have risen a modest 0.3 percent in March for a 4.3 percent year-on-year rise. "While sales are buoyant, consumers still appear to be price conscious," said Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets. She backed the consensus forecast but said weaker numbers would be no surprise.

As for the five-year auction of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002, traders had expected the Bank of England to try and ship out either 2.5 or 3.0 billion pounds of stock, so a mere two billion should prove no trouble.
"They could have got away with selling a bit more than that," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
He expected the auction to attract cover of more than two times.
The only possible problem is the proximity of May 1 elections. That could put overseas investors off, dealers said.

"People feel there's good value there but obviously in a week before an election there's some uncertainty," said Darren Winder, economist at SBC Warburg. "But I would be surprised if there was cover of less than two."
The existing 2002 gilts were trading at 98.81 late on Tuesday, down from Monday's 98.86 Monday close, to yield 7.28 percent.
"These short maturity gilts have cheapened up recently and with only 2.0 billion stg for sale the auction should not be a problem," said Joanne Collins, bond analyst at Nomura.
The 10-year gilt/Bund spread pushed out to 188 basis points from 184 late on Monday.
Traders said rumours of an ICM opinion poll for the Guardian newspaper, due out overnight, showing a sharp cut in Labour's lead to eight percent, had sent a few shivers around the market.
But the Guardian said the poll has not yet been completed.
At the short end of the UK market, June short sterling dropped one basis point to settle at 93.39, just about pricing in a half-point rise in base rates by the end of the first half.
